projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Dante Zarlenga was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II Veteran Dante S. Zarlenga. Mr. Zarlenga served in the U.S. Navy in the European, Mediterranean and Pacific theaters. I'm Tom Swope, and this recording was made at Mr. Zarlenga's home in Mentor, Ohio on December 16th, 2002. Dante was 77 at the time of this recording.

sp.speaker: Dante Zarlenga
sp.p: This first part of this tour was the European theater. I was born in February 13th, 1925, in New York City. My parents came over here from Italy. My brother was born in Italy and he -- nine months later he was here. And in New York, we stayed there two years when we moved to Youngstown, Ohio. So I was really a -- graduated from Rain High School at Youngstown. And the reason why I brought this us is about three or four months before graduation I got a notice to report for duty. And when we got to 'em, I said, "I'm going to graduate." And they said, "Well, we'll let you graduate." July -- June the 11th I graduated, 1943. They rewrote the orders. I got 'em on the 17th of June. And in -- July the 2nd I was in Great Lakes. I mean they didn't waste time. I tell the story that when they gave me the diploma, the Navy was at the other end with the -- "Come on, we need you." I was 18 years old when I went to Great Lakes. Now there is boot camp there. And that was a good training. After the boot camp, from July, somewhere around August I got out of there. We went to Little Creek in Virginia. That's where we got more training. At this point we didn't know what we were going to do other than it's going to be navy. Got more training and finally we ended up -- "Zarlenga you're a signalman." You're this, you're that and you're this. And that's the way it worked.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: No tests or anything like that?

sp.speaker: Dante Zarlenga
sp.p: No. They were tests.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's what you were --

sp.speaker: Dante Zarlenga
sp.p: That's what it came out, that I should be a signalman. And then they -- we still didn't know what we were getting into, and they sent us to Fort Pierce, Florida. Now, that's when we found out we were in an amphibious corp. And we were training on the LCTs, which is landing craft tanks, they call it. And they're a four-man crew: The signalman, machinist that handles the engines, coxswain that drives it, and one guy they call the gunner. But the only guns we had is a holster. You need somebody to tie it up. Yeah, and that's the way it is. And then we practiced down there. It was a vigorous training, with the frogmen. They were involved in this. And when that was all done, we boarded the Liberty Ship. I don't have the right date on that. We boarded the Liberty Ship that was made at -- by Kaiser. Man, they were spitting these out. One of them on -- in fact, they were welding them when they went down to dockin' -- or running these in the water. They were still welding them. In fact, when you're on the sea, sometimes they would crack and welders would be welding it. That's how fast they made these. We boarded one of those. They put our small craft on these and we got into a convoy, a very large convoy, that was going to the Mediterranean. And that was a 17-day zig-zag tour, which meant we didn't want the submarines to know where we were going to end up. Although they found us. And they did find us, but they were waiting to find out where we were going. But they hit a few tankers. And that's about the worst of it. We didn't -- they weren't picking any other ship. They were picking the tankers. I don't know how many of them we got, but when we finally reached the Gibralter -- Gibralter's made like entrance to the Mediterranean was like two big mountains on each side. And you can't have a flotilla this big going through, so they put them in two rows. I was on bridge at the time the message came across from the destroyers. "Stay in line. Do not move to the center. Just stay in line." And the word came out is -- "We have subs that are trying to get in the Mediterranean. Just do not move out of line." And then we were wondering. We're waiting. Everybody's on the deck knowing something's going to happen. Finally, when a lot of these got through, then these destroyers were going up and down dropping their depth charges. I don't think any of them made it, because there was no ship sunk in the Mediterranean. So that was a -- something to watch.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Would this be late 1943?

sp.speaker: Dante Zarlenga
sp.p: That was late in '43. Wait, we were in Palermo. Normandy was in '44.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Dante Zarlenga
sp.p: So it had to be '43. Late in '43 or '44. Because then we get -- Normandy was in June, so this had to be in that area.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That sounds right, yeah.

sp.speaker: Dante Zarlenga
sp.p: Yeah. Those are the dates I don't have. It was actually nine months from the time I got in to the Normandy invasion.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Dante Zarlenga
sp.p: So once we got into the Mediterranean, our first stop was Northern Africa. And I do remember when -- when I would go anywhere, I go to visit -- sightseeing. I don't go to bars or anything. But the -- friend of mine, Norman Zeis, is from Carey, Ohio. We just -- that's all we'd do is just go visit. So we went to the Cazbar. I heard so much about that place. The guide would only take five. He said the reason why is I can't lose anybody in there. You will not come back. "Oh, that's good." We're hugging each other going through, you know. "No, that's all right. Stay close." Then he starts telling the story. He said, "When the police chase somebody in the Cazbar, they stop right here. There's no sense going in, you'll never find them. They could run across the roofs there. They just lose it. And if they want to get rid of anybody in this Cazbar, they just throw them in the streets, the rats will eat them up." You know, that's hard to believe that. And he says, "When we're down in there, we're going to take you into one of the buildings." They're -- I mean, you talk about slums. "We're going to take you in. I got the right to go in, and you're going to see something you won't believe." And then we didn't. It was plush, tapestry, gold all over. And the sheik living there. The front, they don't care. But inside, it was a big, nice place. Couldn't believe it. And he said this -- these are the guys that rule this place. And there's nobody that will live in there, if they don't want you to. And then, well, that was interesting. And then we went to Palermo, Sicily. We got beached there. Or trips, visits, whatever. And then we ended up in Naples. And that's where we had the longest wait ever. The ships were -- I know later on why it was so long. We were setting up an attack group for France. But it was a long time. And I didn't have the exact dates. And of course we got to go to the beach a lot. The beach -- the city. And those poor people there -- I'm Italian. And to see them begging for food was where it hurt. So, my friend and I -- I asked him if he would help me. We could have got discharged for doing this, but we were taking food out to them. Not food. We didn't steal the food. It was food we were going to eat and we just didn't eat it. Whatever we could take, we brought it out to 'em. To see a father selling his daughter, you know, it's amazing. It's hard to believe. I always said: "America doesn't know what war is, other than that civil war. You don't know what you have to go through." Because that would be later, but that was what really woke me up. And then I run into a Army friend from Youngstown, Ohio. He said, "Dan, how would you like to see your grandmother?" Shhew. "Boy, that would be nice. Why?" He said, "I'm going to get a Jeep. Tomorrow morning I'll pick you up early. Can you get" -- "Yeah. I can get off. We can get off anytime we want." He goes, "I'll be here. About eight o'clock. I'm dressed in my whites. Saluted the officer on duty, turned around, salute the flag, start walking down the gangway. And they announced -- announcement came over the PA system that -- "All leaves are cancelled. Get back up." At that point they didn't say why, but I knew it was coming. And I waived at him and says, "I can't get off." I remember you -- we wouldn't never tell where you're at. You couldn't. I wrote a letter home. I told my father, "How's Grandma?" He told me later he knew where I was. It was something. And then you could see the flotilla building up. And finally the word came to go. So we were in Naples. And you got to go across the Mediterranean to get to the southern France. We were going to hit southern France when they hit Normandy. That's what we did. The difference was that whether we weren't ready to hit it exactly, I couldn't say, but it was about two days or three days later we hit. Now, when you hit, you stand out there and you -- you could watch them strafing the -- strafing everything they could see on the beaches. Dropping their bombs. The ships firing like crazy over there. And there wasn't that much resistance at that time. So it was our job now to empty the ships. They lowered ours first. We get on and watched these guys climbing down those ropes. That was dangerous. That ship's going like this and you're trying to get off of that ship into the small boat. And they tell you, "Don't tie your helmet, because if you hit the water, it's going to pull your head off." I felt sorry for those guys. And even on the ships, you know, when we got strafed or anything, they had to stay below. But that's the way it works anyhow. So they hit Normandy in June. I think it was around June 6th or somewhere like that. And about two days later, we were -- we were really going into southern France. We had the LCT's, the landing craft tanks they call them now. All we carried in was troops, ammunition, Jeeps, miscellaneous things. And then bring back their wounded to the ships. But we never did bring a tank in. We could have, but the -- our job was to take these small boats. We had -- the troops were the hardest thing. We hit these small boats. And once you land into the beach, you got to keep the engine running and keep that driving into the beach, because if it turns on you, it's going to be hard to get off. We had -- we had boats that were turned, because their engines conked out. We had -- we lost some boats that time. We were like sittin' ducks. I mean the batteries on the beach, we were just picking them off, you know. Of course we were traveling, but you -- we're not zigging, we're going straight in. So you could see some of your friends. And I got pictures of some that's -- that's tough. Now, as -- like I said, we were sitting ducks. They made a joke. They said, "Dan, don't wave your flag. I don't care what kind of signals you're giving, you're going to make the guy try to get us."

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That was part of your job, was to --

sp.speaker: Dante Zarlenga
sp.p: Yeah. We -- we talked to each other going down, what we were going to do, what ship to go to and ship up to -- your ship might give you directions and what beach. You load up. You just don't load up and go in, you wait for a crew. And then you go into a certain beach, because you got to all hit that beach at the same time. And, you know, like Normandy had different color beaches. So we went from -- we weren't all the way up to Nice, but we were within -- down to Marseille, that whole section of beach in there. And then below that was Toulon. It was -- anyhow. Once we got through with that, later on in life when I watched these movies about the invasions of France, but when I saw this thing, I said that's not northern -- that's not Normandy. That's southern France. And it was. And it was -- we got to see our ships going in and out, the movies and that. Then we found out that's where Audie Murphy's army was. He went in there and he says we probably brought him in. It's either the First or Seventh Army. I didn't remember. I said, "We brought that guy in there." I took my wife one day. I said, "You know, that's where we hit." I wonder. I didn't know him then and I don't know him now, but it was good. Then in France, if things got quiet, we still go off the ship. Mind you they're still fighting inland, the soldiers were. Now, in this here, we -- we ate on the beach with the soldiers. Because we didn't have a -- we had a ship that delivered us there, but that's all. So we were actually eating with the soldiers. And they always joked about us. "Is this better than that stuff you guys get." "Yeah. It's better right now. We're not getting anything over there." Good friends. And then I heard De Gaule was going to be in Marseilles -- Marseilles. So this Norman Zeis and I took off for Marseilles. We were able to see. But we were so far behind we took pictures. I got some in there. All those people all over, but he was there. And another thing that was very interesting, the people back home don't believe what those people went through, like the French. We heard about a -- they were going to call this firing squad. The Free French were going to kill some German collaborators. "Yeah," I said, "Let's go see this." You know, young guys. What do we know? "Let's see. I want to see this." I don't think I'll go to another one. No pictures were ever allowed to be taken. You lined up there and they bring these guys that -- just like you see in the movies. There's a pole there and they hang them on a -- just put the poles in the ground, six of them, or four, whatever, and they bring these old, young, it doesn't matter. And we stood there and watched. He gave the order. And about six or eight of them lined up and shot the first one. They do one at a time. And then they shoot the other one. And they go down. Holy Christ. And you could see the guy flinching. And then he falls, cut him lose. And then they got a coup de grace. They said the guy that leads this thing goes up with a .45, shoots them each in the head, and they're jumping. I said, "Oh, boy, I'm too young to see this." I left there. We left. I said -- we didn't even see the rest. "I don't want to see the rest." They were getting -- they were mad. They said, "These people helped the Germans." Now, these are the Free French. They wear them bands. They had another thing. I got a picture of it somewhere. The women that were playing with the German officers, collaborating, they picked those up. They walked them through the streets naked. Now, that's the picture we got. They're naked. You can tell they don't want to be there. What they do is shave their head off, send them off in the woods. They can't come back until their hair grows. But I don't know how long that takes. I don't know about wigs at that time or anyhow. But it -- they were vicious when they got to be. We'll show you. Now, that's after the Germans got sent away. The biggest thing I wanted to see was the Toulon submarine pens. That's all I wanted to see. So we had a three-day pass. Norman Zeis and I. We dressed in dungarees with the white hat. We got off three days. Yeah, to get -- the Lieutenant said, "Where are you going three days? This is war." Said, "Oh, it's quiet. We want to go down to the submarine pens." "Well, you're okay, if you can keep along the beach." So we did. Hitched a ride. There was no problem getting down. It was a long way. We finally got there, hitchin' rides. And we went into the submarine pens. And they were cut right into the rock. I mean there was about six of them. They'd drive the -- steer their subs right in there, unload, do what they have to. But they can't be bombed. They're too far in. Clever. So we had nothing to do but look around. There were no subs there. We just started looking around for what we could find. I found a German helmet. Also the regular one, the one with the back and the cap. I found a sword, a bayonet that was -- the whole back was notched. That guy was busy. And then I picked up an 1832 dueling pistol. I was trying to find it for you and I don't even know where it's at.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: But you sent all that stuff home?

sp.speaker: Dante Zarlenga
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah. I got it here. And my friend brought back some stuff too. And we went out and says, you know, that was good for looking outside. Finally we got shots come right across our -- right past us. You can feel it. And hit the building. Man, we looked at each other and just took off. So we ran up the way. Now, here's the road. There's a road along the Mediterranean and then another road that cuts off to the left. So when we ran up beside -- we saw this truck coming by that was full of Australians. We knew that when we got in it. "Come on, get in, Yanks." Got in that. And he says, "We're going this way. Where do you want to go?" I said, "Well, our ship's up here." He said, "Well, we can take you up to our camp and you can cut across from there." And went to the camp. That's the only truck, there's nobody going down there. We get up to their camp, "Come on in, have something to eat. Stay with us." "No, we got to get back." So we do. Took off. Followed the same street going inland, same road. First night we slept out, it was cold. It was getting cold then. And wanted to eat. We'd grab grapes that are hanging over the side. The reason why we didn't go across the fence to the farms, my friend said, "Look at the apples and the peaches." I said, "Yeah, but look at those skull and bones in there. They got wires in the ground. Those are mines. You want to take a chance, you throw them out to me," I said. "No, you go get them. And then if you come back, then I'll go." Anyhow, we didn't go. We just kept eating grapes. First night. Second night we're going in. Second day we're still walking. We're walking now. There's not that many Jeeps or anything going by. And then we come across an oil truck. They're not like the trucks you see here. They got something in the back of the truck where you could stand on. It wasn't big. It was an old truck. And the guy -- "Get in the back. Hang on." So we were on the back hanging on. And he was going to take us up. Boy, this is lucky. We get up to a little bridge that crosses a ravine. Two Free French now -- when they stopped the truck, I looked and I saw the bands again -- pulled that guy out, unmercifully beat him. He could have never driven that truck again. They were beating him like I said -- I looked at him, I said, "You know, I don't think I want to go out that way. They don't know us up here." He said, "There's one thing we can get away. They're so busy with this guy. There's only two or three guys beating him up. We'll get off this side and we'll go down. Don't cross the bridge. We'll go down the ravine and up the other side. I don't think they'll see us. But if they do, we'll take our chances." That's what we did. Got to the other side. And we never did know what happened to that poor guy. Of course maybe he was helping the Germans. And we kept going. That's another night we slept. More grapes. The one night it was so cold we were hugging. We were dressed just like you would -- just the dungarees shirt. No coats. We were hugging each other to keep warm. They had a -- what do you call a Stars and Stripes paper in those days to tell you about the war. You could learn all about the war just by reading that. If the Germans get that, they'd know what we were doing. They knew of -- I remember there was a map on the back showing exactly where we hit and how we went in. And -- well, I woke up and he wasn't there. I said -- and finally I heard somebody in the bushes coming back. I literally had a -- started hiding. Then it was him. I said, "Where in the world did you go?" He says, "Well, I had to go to the bathroom." "There's no bathrooms here." He said, "You know what I mean." "What did you use to clean?" He said, "I had that Stars and Stripes." "Oh. Did you use it all?" He said, "No, I ripped it in half." "Let me see the other half." The map was still there. That's how we knew where we were. And then when he saw the map, I said, "If we reach this point, we can go straight to Nice. That's the only road that goes around. Once we get to Nice, we can get into -- go down and get on our ship." All right. There was -- keep on going. We come to a small town. Women with machine guns were watching the streets. I mean, these are -- machine guns are hanging down their -- and the biggest dog I ever saw. Looked big then, anyhow. But the dog didn't bark at us. But -- it was too late there. We walked up. We can't be -- we got to walk up. We don't know who these are. We're stuck. Go on, we talk a little bit Italian I knew. A lot of them knew a little English. Enough that we understood each other. All I had to do was say, "American Navy." "American! Yeah!" They're hugging us and everything. "Come. Come. Come." They thought we were bringing the troops behind us or something. "Come on with us. Come on with us. We're going to eat." All we wanted was water. "Aqua. Aqua." "No, no, no. Vino. Vino." Tell her I don't want wine, I want water. We ate. We had a good time. Finally, we said, "We got to go." "Avanti. Avanti." Okay. And they came down and they hugged us and everything. "Bye-bye." And away we go. And somebody's watching the other side and they're hugging us. I said, "We ought to stay here, you know. We're safe here." And we're going up -- this little map showed there was a little airfield. It showed a plane, so I assume it was just a small plane. I said, "You know, this is getting -- we're in our third day. We're only allowed three days, you know." "Yeah." Says, "I got an idea, Zeis. Let's go to that airfield. How much money you got." "What do you have in mind?" "Pay that guy whatever we got, fly us near the ship, drop us in, we'll just swim to the ship. Somebody will pick us up." "No way am I going to have them drop me in no water." He said, "I can't swim. Not only that," he said, "they'll shoot 'em down." "Oh, no. All right. You're right." We kept on going. And then we come up right at that corner where the sign "Nice" -- there's a road pointing down there. We got there early in the morning. And we saw a guy getting out of a bus that was a burned out bus. He must have slept in it all night. And he had the Free French. We went up to him. He didn't run away. He came over to us. We started talking. "Nice. Aqua. We go to Nice, to a ship." "No, no, no. Nice occupied. Nice is occupied." Geez. The stupid kids. That's what I thought of us at all this. How stupid we were and lucky. We were going to drive right into them and take 'em all. We had no firearms with us or nothing. We wouldn't have used them anyhow. At any rate, that was the -- oh, we did get back. We decided to go back the same way. Picked up rides and walked again. And we were late. We got back. When we finally got to the ship, the Lieutenant -- when we came aboard, they called the Lieutenant right away. He said, "You two guys come with me. Tell me where you were." He wouldn't believe it. He just would not believe it. He said, "You was whorin' around. You were out there with the women, weren't you?" "No, sir. We didn't even think of them. Not once. We went out sightseeing. This is what we saw." "No. I don't believe it. You want to know something. You know that today I wrote up a Missing in Action for you two guys? You're already AWOL. I don't know what I'm going to do with you." He says, "Well, it's a stupid thing, there's no doubt about it. But it's over. It'll never happen again." He says, "Not -- not on my watch, it won't." Anyhow the Germans surrendered in 19 -- May 7th or 8th -- somewhere -- 1945, and we got out 30-days leave to come home. And then they said, "You'll get papers then." So, visit the family for 30 days. That's always tough when you have to leave. Then we had the papers to go to Baltimore. Baltimore. Our ship, by the way -- this is the Pacific theater now. Our ship was the USS Vinton. We were -- we had orders to board the USS Vinton. Was commissioned AKA-83. And it was named after a congressman back in 1772, is when he was born. So it was back in 1800s. He was a congressman. Sam Finley Vinton, from Ohio. And it was commissioned Attack Cargo. It's ship, but it's amphibious. And that was back in February the 23rd, 1945. And the town Vinton is in the small town in south Ohio. Which was odd. So that ship was being built when we were over in Europe. Anyhow, on March the 27th we sailed from Norfolk. And our John Hoffman was the Commodore. And he was USNR, which is reserve. I think he was a merchant marine man. On the 17th, let's see. We left on the 27th of March. We went to the Pacific through the Panama Canal. April the 2nd we were at the Panama Canal and at Pearl Harbor on April the 17th. On May the 1st we were assembling another convoy that was approximately 20 ships. And then we left Honolulu on May the 30th. And June the 1st, now, we were on our way. And don't know where we were going at that time. But on June the 1st, a man named R. H. Smith came aboard. Well, we had to bring him aboard. It was a medical emergency. A submarine had an appendix problem with this guy and they couldn't operate. And so they brought him on our ship. And that submarine was the Silversides, SS-236. Now, that was on June the 1st. And on June the 13th we were at Guam. And that's when he recovered and returned to his ship. So from June 1st -- on the 8th we were at -- in Enewetok Atoll -- Atoll, Marshall Islands. 13th, we were at Guam, Mariana Islands. 26th we were in the Ulithi Lagoons, Caroline Island. And then July 14, Higashi Bay and Okinawa.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What were your missions for most of those --

sp.speaker: Dante Zarlenga
sp.p: We just -- we just reached going somewhere, is all it was.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That was on your way.

sp.speaker: Dante Zarlenga
sp.p: We didn't see anything that we were -- of course they boarded -- they loaded something. I didn't know what it was. But in Okinawa -- the reason why I went this route, on the 19th there was typhoon hit Okinawa. It was the worst typhoon I've ever seen. I haven't seen any, but I don't never want to be in another one. That typhoon, when it was ready to hit, the ships that were anchored were told to weigh anchor and get in a circle and stay in a circle. But it was a big, large circle. But keep moving. I was on watch. And that Lieutenant comes over and says, "You know you're on watch?" I said, "You're kiddin'. What am I going to see? I can't see you in front of me." And you can't. It was that bad. I said, "What do you want me to do?" He said, "Put me glasses -- you stand on this bridge. You watch the ship in front of you, if you can." "What do you want me to do, if I see it?" I mean, I'm a kid yet. Yell, what? He says, "No, you're on watch, and that's your duty." I swore I was telling people this story. I said, "We're 60 feet in the air. And when that ship would swing over to the side, I swear I could do this to the water, you know." That's the way I thought -- maybe the water was coming up. And they tied me to the rail up there, because I would have never stood it. That's the time when I decided I ain't staying in this Navy. To be on watch, at a time like this. They had ships that didn't weigh anchor that were on the beach. That literally -- and that's where they stayed. Back when I worked, after this was all over, and I told this story, a guy I worked with said, "Were you there?" "Yeah. Where were you?" He said, "I was a Marine on the beach." He said, "I couldn't -- I don't understand how you guys lived out there, how you got through that thing, it was so bad." We found out that the Pittsburgh, Battleship Pittsburgh -- this is what I was told. So I didn't see it -- Lost it's bow there. And that thing probably came up like that so big, and when it came down, it just swept the bow. Didn't sink it, because they're all cut off. And they got back into -- I don't know where they took them to fix the bow, it was all right. I don't think they lost anybody. And that was ridiculous to be on watch. And after that, we had another convoy we set up. Now it's getting touchy. The USS Vinton, our ship, was the convoy commodore. They put the Commodore on the ship. I guess they put him on different ships so nobody knows. But he had our ship. Now, during that convoy was where we really saw kamikaze at its best. When they lost all their -- when they shot everything up they could, then they dove right into the ships. We didn't get hit. They were going for the bigger ships, so we didn't get anything. But we got strafed pretty good. I recall -- I don't know whether that was here or in the Liberty. I think it was the Liberty ship. I'm ahead of myself. But I remember we were strafed at the -- our ship was strafed. And this Zeis and I were on the bridge. We saw 'em coming. We both ducked down behind -- you know, there's a rail there and we both ducked down behind that. When he went over, I looked at him, he looked at me, and I says, "Do you know what we just ducked behind?" Canvas. They had canvas down there. "Do you feel better now?" Oh, geez. Kids again. Well, that convoy was en route to Pearl Harbor. We went -- coming back for somethin'. It says with a secret route, and just came off of that. Into Pearl Harbor on August the 6th and 9th. We were waiting for the orders. We were waiting for orders. Japan surrendered August 15th. That's '45. We got confidential orders. Now, mind you, August -- September the 22nd, we got confidential orders, and we were en route. Nobody knew what they were. We're not -- in fact, I got a letter somewhere in there that explains it, where we were going. It's confidential. You're to be quiet. Don't tell anybody about that. And during that trip we passed Wake Island, stopped at Guam. We left Guam at a zig-zag course again. Went to Milne Bay, New Guinea, still wondering where we're going. And then we left Milne Bay. Ended up December the 11th at Batavia, Java. That was a secret destination. They had a civil war going on, and we could not dock to unload. They wouldn't let us to come in. So the 18th to the 24th -- mind you, we were there on the 11th. The 18th to the 24th, we discharged the cargo, at anchor, onto barges, because our captain said, "Get this unloaded or we're leaving." April 5th, 1946, we arrived at San Francisco. That's that. 24th, we left for New York to decommission the ship. I had enough points to get out in 'Frisco, and that's what I wanted out. I wanted off of this ship. And the guys that got off before me were -- let's say, they were on longer than I was. So I had to bring the ship back. I was the only signalman aboard. So we brought it back through the Panama Canal. We arrived in New York. That's where I took the ship's flag. And that's on March the 15th. On the 16th, it was decommissioned. And I was glad I was smart enough to take the flag. On March -- got an honorable discharge from the Navy with four medals and one invasion battle star for France. The one thing I didn't mention in there was we actually crossed the equator during one of these trips that's Pacific. And if you've never been across the equator and you're on a ship -- especially one of these Navy ships -- look out. The ritual is that the ones, the old timers, that have been across, take over the ship. They literally raised the union jackets of skull and bones. The captain is locked in his room. He can't come out. He has no control of the ship. The crew takes over. And, boy, do they take over. Now, they pick guys like us, the greenhorns. What they did is they literally saved the slop that we had for the whole month -- and I mean it was pretty raw by the time we're going to get it. Then they throw oil in these half tubs. They're barrels. They cut them in half and put them along in a stream. And they put this in with oil and water and mix it. And you got to crawl over -- over one bar, under the other bar, over. And every time you come up, somebody whacks you. And then you get hosed down by a fire hose. I mean, they didn't allow any pictures of that thing. But then they give you -- and I got it in here, I'll show you. They give you the certificate that you did it. Now, next time I go across, somebody else is going to get it. They don't have to worry, because I'm not going to be there anyhow. I enjoyed every bit of it. Now. On that deal there, we had a signalman that was a little guy, but he's been on those ships for so long, there's hashmarks all over. He was shaping a -- he called it a shillelagh. And I said, "What are you going to do with that?" He said, "When you guys go through, you'll feel it. You'll know what it is." I made a joke like, "Not if I get it first." Somebody threw it over. You know who got blamed? But it come down, what you have to do is go up to King Neptune, was one of 'em. And he happened to be King Neptune. And he's there with a belly button open and greasy. And you got to kiss this grease. And he says, "Now, why is he here?" Blah, blah, blah. "I know this man, he takes the maximum punishment." "Why?" "You threw my shillelagh over." "I did not do it. I did not do it." He goes through three times. Keeps lying. "I did not throw it over." So I did. Three times I went through that thing. When I got all through, I still don't know who threw that over. I bet it was my buddy. Anyhow it was all -- everybody cleans up and you got your letter. Nobody was hurt. The deck was greasy though. I said, "What do you do with all that stuff?" Man, you -- you talk about some of these guys getting sick going through that, you know, because you -- it's all over your face and everything. I said, "This is punishment. This is nothing else." Anyhow, that's pretty much it. But that's the first one we had. Four of us stopped in 'Frisco. END OF SIDE ONE, TAPE ONE; BEGIN SIDE TWO, TAPE ONE. SWOPE: So the Vinton was an amphibious -- ZARLENGA: Attack --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -- attack cargo?

sp.speaker: Dante Zarlenga
sp.p: Attack auxiliary -- attack amphibious, I guess you would call it. They called it attack cargo ship.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Dante Zarlenga
sp.p: But it isn't a ship. A ship you can't put on another ship, a boat, you know. It's a boat. So it's landing craft tank. But an AKA is attack cargo, which means they carry cargo. Which is -- and it's during invasions. And that's mainly what we did. Now, that must have been that 30-day trip, these old buddies. I used to be a drummer. I had my own band. I played in football for Rain.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, yeah?

sp.speaker: Dante Zarlenga
sp.p: I had my own band. Yeah, small band.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you do anything like that when you were overseas?

sp.speaker: Dante Zarlenga
sp.p: Now, that's another trick. When we got to the boot camp, my buddy fixed me up good. Somebody said, "There any drummers here?" I didn't want that job. He said, "Yes. He does. He plays the drums." Well, they -- well, they did a marching song, and I had to beat the drums for them. I said, "I'll fix you." Now, secret mission. Batavia. "The Vinton is now proceeding on a secret mission the exact nature of which is not known by any officer or man aboard this ship. This is sent so as to avoid any embarrassing situation which might arise from this mission. The following precautionary measures will observe at all options." Now I know why.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Dante Zarlenga
sp.p: We should not have been there. Because they knew there was a civil war. "All U.S. Mail, which has been posted in the post office since leaving Manus, will be returned to the same sender for personal censorship."

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Dante Zarlenga
sp.p: "If and when movements of the vessels at the second are released by the Navy department, you will be notified so that you may write about it thereafter. Each officer and man will sign and obtain a pledge of honor and return to your post office." Now, this was a Senator that wrote it. In Washington today. "The Associated Press announced that Senator George, Democrat of Georgia, told the Senate he was informed that ships sent to bring American soldiers from New Guinea had been ordered" --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Dante Zarlenga
sp.p: -- "on the arrival to load cargo for the Dutch Indies. This is inexcusable. It is unpardonable. It is even criminal. George said he was advised by the ensign in a letter from a friend."

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wow. So they were out trying to aid one of the sides in the civil war?

sp.speaker: Dante Zarlenga
sp.p: I'm not sure what it was. When we lived there, that's all we said, "What are we doing here?"

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Dante Zarlenga
sp.p: That's all. But they kept it quiet. They didn't want the press to know, I think.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Sounds like they --

sp.speaker: Dante Zarlenga
sp.p: But who gave the order?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Dante Zarlenga
sp.p: Now, see if there's one of the shows we put on. I tell you when --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do a lot of shows?

sp.speaker: Dante Zarlenga
sp.p: Well, every time there's something going on, he and I, we come up with something. We cut a -- we had a board on a teeter-totter. You know you jump on one and the guy flips the other one.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Dante Zarlenga
sp.p: I don't know. I think -- yeah, he was going to stand on this -- this side. And I was going to jump off the chair and hit this thing and then he's going to flip.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Dante Zarlenga
sp.p: But the other guy over there holding the chair -- you've seen this thing done.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Dante Zarlenga
sp.p: And he's standing on that chair, on that platform, and I'm up -- say, "When." And I was ready. He runs up and moves the guy a little bit this way. And I jump. Pow. We had cut the board almost in half. And the thing just snapped.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, great.

sp.speaker: Dante Zarlenga
sp.p: And he says, "Not me. Not me." That's the good part of that. Really, the guys. Another thing on that ship, you'd have work deals, work details.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Dante Zarlenga
sp.p: And we found out we were going to be on a nasty one. So he says, "Yeah, let's hide." "Where are you going to hide on a ship?" I said, "I found a place. It's inside the smoke stack." "Are you kidding?" I said, "No. There's two areas. There are the outside and the inside. We can get into that one door and stay in there and nobody looks in there." We did. Everything worked out. We didn't have the detail. Next day we got double detail. "You guys hid somewhere and I couldn't find you. Well, you're going to pay." I said, Boy, that would be different if I took dope. They didn't have dope at those days. We didn't drink or anything. Didn't smoke. I remember too when we took this trip to Toulon, since we didn't smoke, we were allowed to buy the cigarettes for nothing. We bought packs of them. And we were going to sell them outside for twenty dollars a pack. Hell, we probably paid a buck. So we decided to bring them out, slip them out in your -- that's against the law, you know. So we bet. We hitched a ride on a truck, a Jeep. There were two soldiers in it and a third one in the back. Well, the Jeep got stuck. The thing is they didn't -- they pulled the three guys out and searched them. They didn't bother us. We must look like a clean-cut. And I'm looking at these guys, says, "Boy, are we in trouble." I said, "There you go again, Zeis, getting us in trouble again." He said, "You're the one who wanted to get rich." Well, they didn't trounce us. But what we did is we went over and dumped the cigarettes after we got out of there. Said, "This ain't worth it. We don't smoke, what do we need them." Now, see, that just came up. But all of that stuff and then you still -- you try to forget what you saw. When I tell them here about how they lived in Italy -- and not only there. That's wherever the war is. France, they're all the same. I think I even put it on some of those e-mails. V-mails they called them. I said, "I hope that you never see what we're seeing here." But I guess, you know, when you're there, you're there for a reason. You get it done and the rest you're there until you get out. That's really the way it worked. You go wherever they tell you, do whatever they tell you. Then after all of that, that trip down to Batavia, I said, "By, God, we could have got shot out of the water and the war's over." I think that's why they had such a problem in the congress. I don't know if they did anything with that. That would be interesting to find out. There's got to be some records somewhere.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Dante Zarlenga
sp.p: Somebody got it. But it was all work in there. It was all work. You're on that ship, boy, you got to keep it clean just to keep you busy. That's why they did it. Keep the people busy. Don't let them lay around. And we used to watch those guys practice. Like the soldiers would practice coming off of those nets into the boats. Boy, that was sad. Some of those guys get -- missed the rung and they'd fall over backwards or hang -- their foot hangs into the rung. It's not a ladder. It's a --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right. It's a netting.

sp.speaker: Dante Zarlenga
sp.p: -- honeycomb kind of a rope. Everybody's -- about four or five coming down. And you're carrying these rifles on their back. I said, "Oh, my." And we're down below there trying to help 'em in. That's what -- that's when somebody gets hurt. We had another accident on the ship. The guy was using a screwdriver. It's one of the long ones, because he was tightening something. I don't know why he was doing that thing at that time, but the ship must have lurched or somewhere and he's -- that thing slipped, and I think he stuck himself in the face. I was going to say the eye, but I don't think it was eye. I didn't see him. In his face, cripes. I think he fell is what it was, and that thing must have hit him. You know, I just don't know. If I ever hear of or think of anything else.
